dok_rationale: Part (c) weighs two claims against the full data and a contextual threshold, and explains how excluding valid observations changes the conclusion.
stem: Suppose a school newspaper records last night's sleep for 12 students in one class. All 12 values are valid. For this class, the school flags a sleep concern if more than $20\%$ slept fewer than 6 hours.\par\smallskip \textbf{Claim 1:} ``The full table shows a sleep concern in this class.''\par \textbf{Claim 2:} ``Leave out the two lowest sleep values and there is no sleep concern.''
first_take: Which claim, if either, would you print? Name one detail behind your choice.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Name the variable and its unit.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the percent who slept fewer than 6 hours using all 12 students. Then leave out the two lowest values and find the new percent.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Which claim would you print? Use both percents and the school's rule. Explain why keeping or removing the two values changes what readers learn about this class.

answers.a: Hours of sleep last night for each student in this class.
answers.b: All data: $3/12=25\%$. Removing 4.5 and 5.0 hours leaves $1/10=10\%$ below 6 hours.
answers.c: Print Claim 1: $25\%$ exceeds the $20\%$ threshold. Claim 2's $10\%$ is arithmetically correct for the shortened table, but excluding two valid low values changes both the count and the total. It hides part of the sleep concern in the original class.

expectedElements.description: Supports Claim 1 using 25 percent versus the 20 percent rule
Recognizes 10 percent describes the shortened table, not all 12 students
Explains how removing valid low-sleep observations hides the original concern

scoringGuide.E: All three elements are correct and linked to this problem. Accept equivalent plain-language reasoning.
scoringGuide.P: At least one element includes a correct evidence-to-reason link, but another is missing or incorrect.
scoringGuide.I: No correct evidence-to-reason link; only a choice, copied numbers, or unsupported statements.

commonMistakes: Dividing by 12 after removing two students
Calling the shortened percent an arithmetic error rather than a changed data set
Treating a valid low value as permission to omit it
